Thirty-six comments

Reel With the Burl

This version comes off of Martin Hayes’s The Lonseome Touch. The abcs and dots won’t do it justice--you’ve got to hear it to pick up the heavy swing Martin gives it, and to make sense of all those long notes in Part B. Similarly, the fnatural to fsharp in measure 2 of Part B is just a chromatic slide into the g--listening to the recording will help with timing.

No, emphatically!

No, in spite of the very similar first part, the B part is completely different from Drowsey Maggie. But these are merely superficial observations. There is something about this tune which makes me play it very differently -- much less drive, more swing. There is much more to the tunes than the notes. Even changing the key of a tune may make for a totally different approach to it and making it, at least to my ears, a different tune entirely.

Reel With The Birl

X:6 from the piping of Willie Clancy. The asterisk marks where he slurred up into the C natural, for that piping nyah. Willie played actual birls, or crans, rather, on the low E notes at all times - in the Dance Music of Willie Clancy Pat Mitchell added an ‘R’ where Willie played a roll instead of a cran on the low E. Also Willie’s title for this was the Lady’s Bonnet.

↳ Posted by Donough on June 4th, 2014.

The tune with an adopted title “Reel with a Birl”

This tune may have never really had an original title but somehow, maybe it was the Chieftains, it was named a generation or two after it was exclusive to West Clare as “The Reel with the Birl”. 12 years ago it was questioned and denied whether it was a version of Drowsy Maggie. But interestingly no one transcribed one of the first and oldest versions which was recorded of Patrick Kelly in his beautiful archaic style. I have a concert recording of Bobby Casey playing it as well. Bobby’s rendition was much closer to Patrick Kelly’s than any of the ones above though they have a different bow style. Their version I prefer and play. And I prefer Willie Clancy’s title The Lady’s Bonnet. But a tune title is only like a hat while the tune itself is the head….

↳ Posted by jamadairg on June 9th, 2015.

What is The Birl?

I’ve just discoverd that in Scotland and Shetland, the “ birlin’ ” means spinning around with one’s partner [Peter Cooke, The Fiddle Tradition of the Shetland Isles; also “Scottish Country-Dance Dictionary”, https://www.scottish-country-dancing-dictionary.com/birl.html ].
So that adds another possible explanations to those given, e.g., in The Fiddler’s Companion
(https://www.ibiblio.org/fiddlers/REE_RH.htm ).

The Reel With The Beryl (Polca an Rí version)

This is the version of the Beryl that Polca an Rí played. I think I derived it from Caoimhín Ó Raghallaigh’s demonstration of the tune (or, rather, some inspiring concepts shown with its help) at his Willie Week workshop. It’s one of the million tunes in Caoimhín’s class that we didn’t even learn but it still stuck in my head!

The Reel With The Birl, X:15

This is transcribed from Mrs. Crotty’s version on Concertina Music from West Clare by Elizabeth Crotty. In this key, it is well-suited for the Anglo concertina because you can use 2 different A keys to do the 3-note “birl” on A. In its original key, the birl is on the E, which isn’t great for C/G Anglo.
One day, I’ll try to transcribe some of the bass doubling that is her signature style, and gives it such a full sound on her album.

↳ Posted by BansheeWailsOverTheMangoPit on December 11th, 2024.

Beryl or birl, a triplet by any other name.

A birl is a Highland bagpipe triplet ornament on low a. It’s used to great effect in “Drowsy Maggie” in both first and second parts in Highland bagpipe settings of the tune in A mixolydian. There are settings in Bm as well, but they don’t have birls, obviously. This album is from the time when the Cheiftains were being spliced into soundtracks for Hollywood, and shows it. The mix is really weird on the 1979 LP I have. Every once in a while I get nostalgic for the Cheiftains, put one of their old LPs on the turn table and remember once again how frustratingly patched together their sets could be.
